n: T

- The frequent focus on the will of God highlights God's control in fulfilling his plan (see {{Ephesians 1:5|1:5}}, {{Ephesians 1:9|9}}, {{Ephesians 1:11|11}}; {{Ephesians 5:17|5:17}}; {{Ephesians 6:6|6:6}}). 

- *God’s holy people*: Literally *the holy ones*, who are devoted to God (see also {{Ephesians 1:15|1:15}}, {{Ephesians 1:18|18}}; {{Ephesians 2:19|2:19}}; {{Ephesians 3:8|3:8}}, {{Ephesians 3:18|18}}; {{Ephesians 4:12|4:12}}; {{Ephesians 5:3|5:3}}; {{Ephesians 6:18|6:18}}). 

- The oldest manuscripts do not include in Ephesus, and there are no personal greetings in this letter. Many scholars think the letter was originally meant to be shared among several churches in the area, not just the church in Ephesus.
T

Paul follows the typical style of ancient Greek letters. He starts with a brief introduction about himself, then offers greetings. However, Paul expands this basic pattern in a distinctly Christian way. 

First, Paul refers to his divine calling as an apostle rather than just stating his name. This shows that his authority comes from God, not from himself.

Second, Paul describes the people he writes to as "God's holy people" and as "faithful followers of Christ." This reminds them of their special identity and relationship with God.
B

Paul greeted the believers and talked about the spiritual blessings they had received.

The believers were part of God’s plan for the world. The blessings helped them understand God’s plan.

Paul described God’s plan in verse 10. God’s plan is to bring together all things in heaven and on earth under Christ. This means that Jesus will have complete authority over everyone and everything.

He already rules in heaven. One day he will rule completely in heaven and on earth. When that happens, the world God created will no longer be separated from God. All of God’s people will be set free from the power of sin and death.

This is what God had planned before he even made the world. Believers already belong to Jesus. They believe that he is the Lord Jesus Christ. They have been adopted into God’s family.

They have the Holy Spirit living inside them and among them. God has done all of this for them because he loves them.
T

Paul often asks for God's grace and peace for his readers. Grace is a blessing from God's kindness that we do not earn. Peace is a feeling of well-being and contentment based on the good news about Jesus and brought by the Holy Spirit (see {{Galatians 5:22|Galatians 5:22}}). Both are gifts from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ (see {{Romans 5:1-2|Romans 5:1–2}}).
T

Paul describes every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms in {{Ephesians 1:4-8|1:4–8}}, {{Ephesians 1:13-14|13–14}}. Paul focuses not on physical blessings, but on what God has done through Christ to save people and bring them closer to him.
T

Paul praises God for all the spiritual blessings given through Jesus Christ to both non-Jewish people (Gentiles) and Jews. This section is a single, complex sentence in Greek. It is one of the longest sentences in Paul’s letters. Long sentences are typical of Paul’s writing (also in {{Ephesians 1:15-23|1:15–23}}; {{Ephesians 2:1-7|2:1–7}}, {{Ephesians 2:14-16|14–16}}; {{Ephesians 3:1-12|3:1–12}}, {{Ephesians 3:14-19|14–19}}; {{Colossians 1:3-29|Colossians 1:3–29}}; {{Colossians 2:1-3|2:1–3}}, {{Colossians 2:8-15|8–15}}). These sentences are interwoven (connected and linked together like threads that are knitted or laced together). This reflects the interconnectedness of their ideas. Interwoven sentences show that different ideas are closely connected and depend on each other.
T

Ephesians has two parts: 

- Chapters {{Ephesians 1:1-3:21|1–3}} praise God for his amazing grace.

- Chapters {{Ephesians 4:1-6:24|4–6}} teach believers how to live in grateful response.
T

God's people are holy and without fault in his eyes because they trust in Christ's sacrifice to atone for their sins (see {{Ephesians 1:7|1:7}}; {{Ephesians 5:25-27|5:25–27}}; {{Colossians 1:22|Colossians 1:22}}; {{Titus 3:5-7|Titus 3:5–7}}; {{Jude 24|Jude 1:24}}).
T

God decided in advance to adopt us into his family. By his sovereign choice, God welcomes and blesses those who trust in Christ as his children. They become heirs to all the promises God made to his people (see {{Ephesians 1:11|1:11}}, {{Ephesians 1:14|14}}; {{Ephesians 2:19|2:19}}; {{Romans 8:15-17|Romans 8:15–17}}, {{Romans 8:29-30|29–30}}; {{Galatians 4:5|Galatians 4:5}}).
T

- Believers praise God, who has blessed them greatly with his forgiving grace. 

- *his dear Son*: This literally means *the beloved,* a title for Jesus as the Messiah; see {{Matthew 3:17|Matthew 3:17}}; {{Matthew 17:5|17:5}}; {{Colossians 1:13|Colossians 1:13}}.
T

- *In him we have redemption through the blood of his Son*: Believers were once prisoners of sin. Now they are free from God's judgment and from the bondage to sin because of Christ's sacrificial death (see {{Ephesians 1:14|1:14}}; {{Ephesians 4:30|4:30}}; {{Romans 3:24|Romans 3:24}}; {{1 Corinthians 6:20|1 Corinthians 6:20}}; {{Colossians 1:14|Colossians 1:14}}; compare {{Matthew 26:28|Matthew 26:28}}; {{Mark 10:45|Mark 10:45}}; {{Hebrews 9:11-12|Hebrews 9:11–12}}, {{Hebrews 9:26|26}}; {{1 Peter 1:18-19|1 Peter 1:18–19}}).
T

Wisdom and understanding come from God revealing his mysterious plan about Christ. In Paul's writings, *mysterious will* (traditionally *mystery*) often means a divine truth once hidden but now revealed in the good news (see {{Ephesians 3:9|3:9}}). Here, it refers to how God will unite everything under Christ's authority, so he is universally recognized and respected as Lord (see {{Philippians 2:9-11|Philippians 2:9–11}}; {{Colossians 1:16-20|Colossians 1:16–20}}, {{Colossians 1:26-27|26–27}}; {{Colossians 2:2|2:2}}, {{Colossians 2:19|19}}; {{Colossians 4:3|4:3}}). Ephesians specifically highlights the inclusion of both Gentiles and Jews in God's redeemed people (see {{Ephesians 3:3-6|Ephesians 3:3–6}}; {{Ephesians 6:19|6:19}}; compare {{Romans 16:25-26|Romans 16:25–26}}).
T

- *In Him we were also chosen as God’s own*: Paul often describes salvation as an *inheritance*, a promise made to our spiritual ancestors and now received by us (see {{Romans 8:17|Romans 8:17}}; {{Galatians 3:29|Galatians 3:29}}; {{Galatians 4:7|4:7}}; {{Colossians 1:12|Colossians 1:12}}; {{Colossians 3:24|3:24}}). 

- God is sovereign (he has supreme power and authority over everything). Because of this, God ensures everything works according to his plan (compare {{Romans 8:28-30|Romans 8:28–30}}).
T
*We* here likely refers to Jews, and *you* likely refers to non-Jews (Gentiles).
T

*you were sealed*: In ancient times, people used seals to mark items as their personal property. Just as a *seal* shows true ownership, the Holy Spirit in a believer’s life shows God’s ownership ({{Ephesians 4:30|4:30}}; {{2 Corinthians 1:22|2 Corinthians 1:22}}).
T

The Spirit serves as both God's promise of future blessings and a preview of eternal life and power. A believer's eternal inheritance includes everything God promised (see also {{Ephesians 1:18|1:18}}; {{Romans 8:17|Romans 8:17}}; {{2 Corinthians 1:22|2 Corinthians 1:22}}; {{2 Corinthians 5:5|5:5}}; {{Galatians 3:29|Galatians 3:29}}; {{Galatians 4:7|4:7}}; {{Colossians 1:12|Colossians 1:12}}; {{Colossians 3:24|3:24}}; {{Titus 3:7|Titus 3:7}}).
T

Paul connects faith in Christ with love for God's people. Personal faith in Christ leads to salvation. Salvation is shown mainly through a life of love (see {{Galatians 5:6|Galatians 5:6}}; {{Colossians 1:4|Colossians 1:4}}; {{1 Thessalonians 1:3|1 Thessalonians 1:3}}; {{1 Thessalonians 3:6|3:6}}; {{1 Thessalonians 5:8|5:8}}; {{2 Thessalonians 1:3|2 Thessalonians 1:3}}; {{1 Timothy 1:14|1 Timothy 1:14}}; {{1 Timothy 2:15|2:15}}; {{Titus 2:2|Titus 2:2}}).
B

Paul had heard about the faith and love of these believers.

He wanted them to know that he prayed for them.

He prayed that they would know God and God’s power. He prayed that they would understand the plan God had for the future.

God’s plan is for Jesus to rule completely over heaven and earth. Paul boldly said that Jesus has more power and authority than anyone or anything. This includes all human rulers. It also includes all spiritual beings.

Jesus is already the ruler of the church.
T
Paul prays that his readers gain the spiritual understanding to fully appreciate God's gifts ({{Ephesians 1:3-14|1:3–14}}).
T

- *a spirit of wisdom*: The word *spirit* can mean the Holy Spirit or the human spirit. 

- Knowing God means having a personal and experiential relationship with him, not just intellectual knowledge (see {{John 17:3|John 17:3}}).
T
Believers confidently hope for Christ's return and the future blessings they will share. United with Christ, they become co-heirs of all God's promised blessings.
T

- God's power for those who believe in him is the power of his Spirit working in and through his people, because they are connected to the resurrected Christ (see {{Romans 6:4-14|Romans 6:4–14}}; {{Colossians 2:12|Colossians 2:12}}). Paul wanted to experience the power of Christ's resurrection in his own life ({{Philippians 3:10|Philippians 3:10}}). 

- In biblical times, the place of honor was always at a person's right hand ({{Psalm 110:1|Psalm 110:1}}; {{Acts 7:56|Acts 7:56}}).
T

*far above:* Jesus has power and authority that is greater than all other powers, whether human or spiritual beings. This includes powers in the present age and in the age to come (see {{Ephesians 3:10|3:10}}; {{Ephesians 6:12|6:12}}; {{John 12:31|John 12:31}}; {{Romans 8:38-39|Romans 8:38–39}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:24|1 Corinthians 15:24}}; {{Colossians 1:13|Colossians 1:13}}; {{Colossians 2:10|2:10}}, {{Colossians 2:15|15}}; {{1 Peter 3:22|1 Peter 3:22}}; {{Revelation 12:7-9|Revelation 12:7–9}}).
T

*under His feet*: In ancient Near Eastern art, victorious kings often placed their feet on the necks of their defeated enemies. Paul uses this imagery to show how Christ has defeated all his enemies and reigns as king over everything (see {{Psalm 110:1|Psalm 110:1}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:25-28|1 Corinthians 15:25–28}}).
T

*the fullness of Him who fills all in all:* This challenging phrase likely means that the church, as his body, fully expresses Christ in this world. His presence, which fills the entire universe, is reflected in and works through his body ({{Ephesians 4:10|4:10}}).
T

Paul describes how the people he was writing to were in a terrible spiritual condition before they believed in Jesus Christ. He says they were like dead people in their relationship with God (see {{Ephesians 2:5|2:5}}; {{Colossians 2:13|Colossians 2:13}}). This spiritual death happened because of their disobedience and sins. They regularly did things that went against God's will and broke his commands.

Paul explains that their sinful actions were influenced by the power of the devil. The devil was working in their lives, leading them away from God and toward wrongdoing.

Because of this situation, the people Paul wrote to were under God's judgment. They were condemned along with everyone else in the world who did not follow God.
B

Before people start following Jesus, they are controlled by sin. Paul described this as being dead. Their bodies are alive but the spiritual side of them is dead.

They live as slaves to the devil. Paul called the devil the ruler of the spiritual forces of evil. He was talking about evil spiritual beings.

On their own, people can’t stop the power that evil has over them. God saves them from sin. He gives them new life that comes through Jesus. God does this because he is kind and full of grace and love.

The work that Jesus did on the cross shows how much grace God has. God has always wanted people to belong to Jesus and to live like Jesus lived. He wants them to do the good works that Jesus taught people to do.
T
Paul thinks about how difficult life was for the believers before they found Christ. He appreciates God's grace for saving them.
T

Human sin is influenced by the devil, also called Satan, who leads the evil spiritual forces that oppose God (see {{Ephesians 1:21|1:21}}; {{Ephesians 6:11-12|6:11–12}}; compare {{Colossians 1:13|Colossians 1:13}}). This same evil spirit also rules over people who refuse to obey God ({{2 Corinthians 4:4|2 Corinthians 4:4}}; contrast {{Romans 8:2-14|Romans 8:2–14}}; {{Galatians 5:22-23|Galatians 5:22–23}}).
T

People who have not converted are naturally controlled by their strong desires and sinful nature (see {{Romans 3:9-20|Rom 3:9–20}}, {{Romans 3:23|23}}). Because of their sin, they are subject to God’s anger, because God hates sin (see {{Ephesians 5:6|Ephesians 5:6}}; {{Romans 1:18|Romans 1:18}}; {{Romans 2:5|2:5}}, {{Romans 2:8|8}}; {{Romans 3:5|3:5}}, {{Romans 3:19|19}}; {{Romans 4:15|4:15}}; {{Romans 5:9|5:9}}; {{Romans 9:22|9:22}}; {{Romans 12:19|12:19}}; {{Romans 13:4-5|13:4–5}}; {{Colossians 3:6|Colossians 3:6}}; {{1 Thessalonians 1:10|1 Thessalonians 1:10}}; {{1 Thessalonians 2:16|2:16}}; {{1 Thessalonians 5:9|5:9}}).
T
By God's mercy, kindness, and love, those united with Jesus Christ are saved from the terrible consequences of their sin and enjoy the benefits of Christ's resurrection.
T

- *made us alive with Christ*: Believers are united with Christ and share in his resurrection, now and in the future (see {{Ephesians 2:6|2:6}}; {{Romans 6:4-14|Romans 6:4–14}}; {{Colossians 3:1-4|Colossians 3:1–4}}). 

- *It is by grace you have been saved!*: See {{Ephesians 1:2|Ephesians 1:2}}; {{Ephesians 2:8-9|2:8–9}}.
T

*And God raised us up with Christ and seated us with Him*: Because of this union, believers share in God's glory and blessings. They experience resurrection both now and in the future (see {{Romans 6:4-14|Romans 6:4–14}}; {{Colossians 2:12-13|Colossians 2:12–13}}; {{Colossians 3:1-4|3:1–4}}).
T
*grace*: Refer to the study note on 1:2.
T

This is a brief summary of how a person is saved. A key belief of the good news about Jesus is that people are made righteous by trusting in Christ. They are not made righteous by their own efforts (see {{Romans 1:16-17|Romans 1:16–17}}; {{Romans 3:24-25|3:24–25}}; {{Galatians 2:16|Galatians 2:16}}; compare {{John 3:16|John 3:16}}, {{John 3:36|36}}). Salvation is not a reward for the good things we have done (see {{Romans 3:21-4:8|Romans 3:21–4:8}}; {{Romans 9:16|9:16}}; {{Galatians 3:2-10|Galatians 3:2–10}}; {{Galatians 5:1-6|5:1–6}}; compare {{2 Timothy 1:9|2 Timothy 1:9}}; {{Titus 3:5|Titus 3:5}}). Salvation is for those who trust only Christ to save them. Therefore, none of us can boast about it (compare {{Romans 3:27|Romans 3:27}}; {{Romans 4:2|4:2}}; {{1 Corinthians 1:30-31|1 Corinthians 1:30–31}}; {{Galatians 6:14|Galatians 6:14}}).
T

*For we are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works:* Good works are the results of salvation. Good works do not cause salvation. God’s Spirit, working through a transformed heart, produces a good life ({{Galatians 5:22-23|Galatians 5:22–23}}).
T

Traditionally, Jews avoided Gentiles and did not consider them part of God’s people. They called them *uncircumcised*, meaning they had not received the sign of the covenant (see {{Genesis 17:9-14|Genesis 17:9–14}}). But Paul taught that it is shallow to judge people based only on outward signs. What matters is a person’s heart and faith. In Christ, physical circumcision does not make someone part of God’s family (see {{Romans 2:28-29|Romans 2:28–29}}).
B

Some of the believers Paul wrote to were Gentiles. They weren’t citizens of the nation of Israel. They lived separated from God.

Other believers Paul was writing to were Jews. They knew about God and God’s covenants. Yet they also lived separated from God because their hearts hadn’t been changed. That is what Paul meant about being circumcised only in their bodies.

Jews and Gentiles also lived separated from one another. Paul described it like a wall of hatred between them. The Holy Spirit works to help Jews and Gentiles believe in Jesus. When people believe in Jesus, they belong to him. Belonging to him means that they are brought close to the Father. This happens through the power of the Holy Spirit.

All Jews and Gentiles who belong to Jesus are citizens of heaven. They are part of God’s family. This is more important than the family or nation that people are born into. They mustn’t let hatred separate them from one another but must live together in peace. Jesus gives them peace with one another and with God.

Believers are like stones in a building. All together they are like a temple and God lives among them.
T

Paul now focuses on the grace God has given, particularly to Gentiles (non-Jews). God brought them into his family and united them with Jews in a new, unified, multiethnic community. This new community is the body of Christ, the church. Paul’s focus on including Gentiles suggests they might have experienced discrimination from Jewish Christians.
T

Before non-Jewish people (Gentiles) became believers in Jesus Christ, they had no part in God’s people or the covenant promises God had made to them. They were without God and without hope (see {{Ephesians 4:18|4:18}}; {{Colossians 1:21|Colossians 1:21}}).
T

A person can only be reconciled to God by being united with Christ Jesus through trust in him (see {{Romans 5:10-12|Romans 5:10–12}}; {{2 Corinthians 5:18-21|2 Corinthians 5:18–21}}). The blood of Christ makes this reunion possible (see {{Ephesians 1:7|Ephesians 1:7}}; {{Romans 3:24-25|Romans 3:24–25}}; {{Romans 5:9|5:9}}; {{Colossians 1:20|Colossians 1:20}}; compare {{Hebrews 9:12-15|Hebrews 9:12–15}}; {{1 Peter 1:19|1 Peter 1:19}}; {{1 John 1:7|1 John 1:7}}; {{Revelation 1:5|Revelation 1:5}}; {{Revelation 5:9|5:9}}). When the Bible talks about "the blood of Christ," it is referring to the death of Jesus as a sacrifice. Through the sacrifice of Jesus, God offers forgiveness and reconciliation to all who believe.
T

- *For He Himself is our peace*: We have peace with God ({{Ephesians 2:16-17|2:16–17}}; {{Romans 5:1|Romans 5:1}}, {{Romans 5:10-11|10–11}}, {{Romans 5:18-21|18–21}}; {{Colossians 1:20-22|Colossians 1:20–22}}). There is also peace between Jews and gentiles (see {{Ephesians 2:15-16|Ephesians 2:15–16}}; {{Ephesians 4:3|4:3}}). 

- *has torn down the dividing wall of hostility*: Social and religious practices traditionally divided Jews from gentiles. A low wall around the temple in Jerusalem marked the boundary that gentiles could not cross. It symbolized the separation Jews maintained from gentiles.
T

- *by abolishing in His flesh the law of commandments and decrees*: See {{Romans 10:4|Romans 10:4}}; {{Colossians 2:14|Colossians 2:14}}; compare {{Romans 6:14|Romans 6:14}}; {{Romans 7:4-6|7:4–6}}. 

- The church is one new people. It is a community where love and acceptance are valued, and ethnic differences do not cause division (see {{Romans 15:7-12|Romans 15:7–12}}; {{Galatians 3:28|Galatians 3:28}}; compare {{John 10:16|John 10:16}}).
T
Christ's death on the cross reconciles humans to God. It also reconciles Jews and Gentiles to each other.
T

- *far away … near*: This verse might refer to {{Isaiah 57:19|Isaiah 57:19}}. 

- The Greek text does not include the words Gentiles and Jews, but they are implied (see {{Ephesians 2:13|Ephesians 2:13}}; see also study note on 1:12–13).
T

Because of Christ’s sacrifice for sins, both Jewish and Gentile believers receive the Holy Spirit. This allows them to approach God openly (see {{Ephesians 3:12|3:12}}; compare {{Acts 10:34-37|Acts 10:34–37}}, {{Acts 10:44-48|44–48}}; {{1 Peter 3:18|1 Peter 3:18}}).
T

Gentiles who believe are no longer strangers and foreigners ({{Ephesians 2:11-12|2:11–12}}, {{Ephesians 2:17|17}}). Through Christ, they are fully accepted into God’s family. They become children of God, just like believing Jews (see {{Romans 8:14-17|Romans 8:14–17}}).
T

- Apostles are missionary evangelists sent by God. They travel to share the good news about Jesus with others.

- Here, the prophets seem to be from the New Testament, not the Old Testament (see {{Ephesians 3:5|3:5}}; {{Ephesians 4:11|4:11}}; see also {{1 Corinthians 12:10|1 Corinthians 12:10}}, {{1 Corinthians 12:28-29|28–29}}; {{1 Corinthians 14:1-5|14:1–5}}, {{1 Corinthians 14:22-24|22–24}}, {{1 Corinthians 14:29-32|29–32}}, {{1 Corinthians 14:39|39}}; compare {{Acts 13:1|Acts 13:1}}; {{Acts 19:6|19:6}}; {{Acts 21:9-10|21:9–10}}). In both the Old and New Testaments, prophets do not primarily predict the future. Instead, they are empowered to speak a message from God (see {{1 Corinthians 12:10|1 Corinthians 12:10}}). 

- *on the foundation of the apostles and prophets:* This means the church is based on their faithful witness to the saving message of Christ (see {{Revelation 21:14|Revelation 21:14}}; compare {{Matthew 16:18|Matthew 16:18}}). However, Christ Jesus himself is the cornerstone, the Messiah, Savior, and Lord (compare {{1 Corinthians 3:11|1 Corinthians 3:11}}). The cornerstone is the most important stone in a building’s foundation (see {{Isaiah 28:16|Isaiah 28:16}}; {{Mark 12:10|Mark 12:10}}; {{Acts 4:11|Acts 4:11}}; {{1 Peter 2:6-7|1 Peter 2:6–7}}).
T

Gentile and Jewish Christians unite in Christ to form a holy temple for the Lord. The Lord is present among his people (see {{Matthew 18:20|Matthew 18:20}}; {{Matthew 28:20|28:20}}; {{1 Corinthians 3:16|1 Corinthians 3:16}}; {{1 Peter 2:4-5|1 Peter 2:4–5}}).
T

- *For this reason*: Paul wrote about the amazing salvation that God's grace brings to undeserving sinners under his judgment. He also wrote about the incredible revelation that gentiles can join God's new family, the people of God (chapters {{Ephesians 1:1-2:22|1–2}}). 

- *the prisoner of Christ Jesus*: Paul wrote this letter while imprisoned for sharing his faith with the gentiles.
B

Paul was in prison even though he hadn’t done anything wrong. He had been put in prison for the work he was doing as an apostle.

God sent Paul to preach the good news about Jesus to Gentiles. This was part of how God was accomplishing his plan for the world. God’s plan was to bring together all things in creation under Christ.

This had always been God’s plan but people hadn’t understood it. Spiritual beings in the heavenly world hadn’t understood it either. That is why Paul called it the mystery of Christ. The mystery was that all people can be near to God through Jesus.

God gave Paul grace and power to share this message. People had put Paul in prison for preaching it faithfully. But Paul didn’t lose hope even though he was suffering. Paul trusted that God would share his glory and unlimited riches with him in the future. Paul wasn’t speaking about receiving money but about spiritual blessings.
T
- Paul explains his special job in God's plan that has existed forever. His role is to announce God's grace to gentiles (non-Jewish people).
T

Paul pauses his thought in {{Ephesians 3:1|3:1}} to talk about his role in God's plan. When Paul first converted, God gave him the special task of sharing his grace with the gentiles (see {{Acts 9:15-16|Acts 9:15–16}}; {{Acts 22:14-15|22:14–15}}, {{Acts 22:21|21}}; {{Acts 26:17-18|26:17–18}}; {{Romans 1:5|Romans 1:5}}; {{Romans 11:13-14|11:13–14}}; {{Romans 15:15-18|15:15–18}}; {{Galatians 1:15-16|Galatians 1:15–16}}; {{Galatians 2:7-9|2:7–9}}; {{Colossians 1:25-27|Colossians 1:25–27}}; {{1 Timothy 2:7|1 Timothy 2:7}}; {{2 Timothy 4:17|2 Timothy 4:17}}).
T

- Paul's earlier writing refers either to {{Ephesians 1:9-10|1:9–10}} (compare {{Ephesians 2:11-22|2:11–22}}) or to an unknown letter. 

- Paul understood God's mysterious plan because God revealed it to him (see study note on 1:8–10; {{Ephesians 1:9-10|1:9–10}}; {{Galatians 1:11-12|Galatians 1:11–12}}, {{Galatians 1:15-17|15–17}}; compare {{Acts 9:3-6|Acts 9:3–6}}; {{1 Corinthians 12:1|1 Corinthians 12:1}}, {{1 Corinthians 12:7|7}}; {{Galatians 2:2|Galatians 2:2}}).
T

- *God's holy apostles and prophets*: See {{Ephesians 1:1|1:1}}. 

- The order of the terms apostles and prophets (see {{Ephesians 2:20|2:20}}) suggests that Paul is referring to New Testament prophets, not Old Testament ones. In both the Old Testament and the New Testament, the gift of prophecy is more about delivering a special message from God than predicting the future (see {{1 Corinthians 12:10|1 Corinthians 12:10}}).
T
God’s plan that has now been revealed to Paul is that the Gentiles are now included in God’s family, the body of Christ, just as Jews are. They share equally in God’s eternal blessings.
T

- *grace*: See study note on 1:2. 

- *I became a servant:* Paul describes himself as a servant of:

- the gospel (see also {{Colossians 1:23|Colossians 1:23}}), 

- of God ({{1 Corinthians 3:5|1 Corinthians 3:5}}; {{2 Corinthians 6:4|2 Corinthians 6:4}}), 

- of Christ ({{2 Corinthians 11:23|2 Corinthians 11:23}}), 

- of the church ({{Colossians 1:25|Colossians 1:25}}), and 

- of the new covenant ({{2 Corinthians 3:6|2 Corinthians 3:6}}).
T

- Paul thought he was the least deserving of all God's people because he once strongly persecuted believers (see {{1 Corinthians 15:9|1 Corinthians 15:9}}; {{1 Timothy 1:12-16|1 Timothy 1:12–16}}). 

- *unsearchable riches of Christ*: See {{Ephesians 1:3-14|Ephesians 1:3–14}}.
T

- The church has an important purpose in God's plan. It is meant to show to the entire universe how wise God is. The church displays God's wisdom in all its rich variety. This wisdom is shown through how God saves people from sin and brings them into his family (see {{Romans 11:33-36|Romans 11:33–36}}). 

- *the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms*: See {{Ephesians 1:21|Ephesians 1:21}} and corresponding study note.
T

We can approach God boldly and confidently. This means we can come into God's presence without fear or hesitation. This boldness in approaching God is not because of the good things we have done. Instead, our confidence comes from Christ's sacrifice for our sins. When Jesus died on the cross, his sacrifice was all-sufficient (see {{Ephesians 2:18|2:18}}; {{Hebrews 4:14-16|Hebrews 4:14–16}}; {{Hebrews 10:19-23|10:19–23}}; {{1 Peter 3:18|1 Peter 3:18}}; {{1 John 4:14|1 John 4:14}}).

*because of my sufferings for you*: Paul writes from jail as a prisoner (see {{Ephesians 3:1|3:1}}). He understands that suffering is to be expected and that it works for good in a believer's life (see {{Romans 5:3-5|Romans 5:3–5}}; {{Colossians 1:24|Colossians 1:24}}; {{1 Thessalonians 3:3|1 Thessalonians 3:3}}; {{2 Timothy 3:12|2 Timothy 3:12}}; {{James 1:2-4|James 1:2–4}}).
T
*… for this reason I bow my knees before the Father*: Paul continues what he began to say at the start of the chapter (see {{Ephesians 3:1|3:1}}).
B

In chapter 2 Paul described how believers are near to God. Paul’s prayer shows how near God is to believers.

The Holy Spirit’s power is deep down inside of believers. Christ lives inside their hearts. And they are filled with everything God has for them.

One of the things that God fills believers with is his love. Paul described the love of Christ as something that is wide, long, high and deep. God’s love has no end and can’t be measured.

Paul made bold requests in his prayer for the believers. Paul knew that God could do much more than what he asked. For this, Paul praised God and gave him glory.
T

Paul ends this section ({{Ephesians 1:3-3:21|1:3–3:21}}) with a second prayer for the people he is writing to. The first prayer in {{Ephesians 1:15-23|1:15–23}} was for their spiritual understanding. The second prayer in {{Ephesians 3:14-21|3:14–21}} is for their spiritual growth and strength.
T

*from whom every family in heaven and on earth derives its name*: There is a wordplay in the original Greek language between the words "Father" (*patēr,* {{Ephesians 3:14|3:14}}) and *family* (*patria*). This wordplay shows a connection between God as Father and all the families that exist. As the Creator of everything, God made all families—both angelic families in heaven and human families on earth. This includes all people groups, whether gentile or Jewish (see {{Ephesians 2:14-22|2:14–22}}; {{Ephesians 3:6|3:6}}). Because God is the Creator of everything, he has access to glorious, unlimited resources. He does not hold back these resources but gladly gives them to his children.
T

*so that Christ may dwell in your hearts*: Having Christ make his home in your hearts is what gives believers spiritual power for life and ministry (see {{John 14:16-17|John 14:16–17}}, {{John 14:23|23}}; {{John 15:4-5|15:4–5}}; {{Galatians 2:20|Galatians 2:20}}).
T
*to comprehend the length and width and height and depth: *Christ's love is great in every dimension (see {{Romans 8:38-39|Romans 8:38–39}}).
T

- *to know this love*: The Christian life is based on experiencing and personally knowing God's grace and love through Jesus Christ (see {{Romans 12:1|Romans 12:1}}). 

- *that surpasses knowledge*: Christ's love is much greater than ordinary human love (see {{Romans 5:6-8|Romans 5:6–8}}). 

- A believer's life becomes complete when filled with the fullness of life and power through Christ's presence (see {{Ephesians 1:23|Ephesians 1:23}}; {{Galatians 2:20|Galatians 2:20}}; {{Colossians 1:27|Colossians 1:27}}). The believer then conforms to his image and reflects God (see {{Ephesians 4:14|Ephesians 4:14}}, {{Ephesians 4:24|24}}; {{Ephesians 5:1-2|5:1–2}}; {{Romans 8:29|Romans 8:29}}; {{2 Corinthians 3:16-18|2 Corinthians 3:16–18}}).
T

*Now to Him … be the glory*: God deserves nothing less because of the grace God has shown through Jesus Christ. The mighty power within us is God's power, which raised Christ from the dead (see {{Ephesians 1:19-20|1:19–20}}). With that power, God can do much more than we ask or imagine, as God works in the lives of his children (see {{Romans 8:31-39|Romans 8:31–39}}; {{Philippians 4:13|Philippians 4:13}}; {{Colossians 1:29|Colossians 1:29}}).
T

A doxology is a statement of praise to God. This doxology ends the first section of Paul's letter to the Ephesians (see also {{Romans 16:25-27|Romans 16:25–27}}; {{Galatians 1:5|Galatians 1:5}}; {{1 Timothy 1:17|1 Timothy 1:17}}; {{2 Timothy 4:18|2 Timothy 4:18}}; {{Jude 24-25|Jude 1:24–25}}). It is Paul's way of praising God for all he has described in these chapters.
T
The church, which is the community of believers including both Jews and Gentiles, should reflect and fully express God's glory.
T

- *As a prisoner in the Lor*d: (see study note on 3:1). 

- Although believers cannot earn salvation, they should live in a way that honors their calling to salvation (see {{Philippians 1:27|Philippians 1:27}}; {{Colossians 1:10|Colossians 1:10}}; {{1 Thessalonians 2:12|1 Thessalonians 2:12}}). 

- *the calling you have received*: (see {{Ephesians 1:4-5|Ephesians 1:4–5}}, {{Ephesians 1:11|11}}).
T
God's saving grace for both Jews and non-Jews (Gentiles) should guide how they interact in the church. They should welcome each other warmly, just as God has welcomed them.
B

Paul made it clear that God is the only God. He is God over everything and everyone that exists. He isn’t the God of only certain groups or certain areas of the world.

All who worship and serve him are brought together as one. They share the same faith in Jesus. Their baptism shows that they all follow him as Lord. The Holy Spirit lives inside each of them. They share the same hope about what God will do in the future.

All of these things that believers share bring them together as one. They are so closely joined to one another that they are like one body. This body is held together through the peace that Jesus gives. It’s held together through truth and love.

Each believer must do the work Jesus has given them to do. They must also be gentle, patient and humble toward other believers. This helps the body of Christ to remain strong.
T

*then*: Ephesians divides into two sections:

- The first explains the good news about Jesus (the gospel).

- The second describes how Christians should live. 

This division reflects Paul's belief about the Christian life. He believed that how Christians live should be a response of gratitude for what God has already done for them through Christ.
T

*with all humility … gentleness … patience*: Believers should be like Christ in how they treat others (see {{Colossians 3:12-14|Colossians 3:12–14}}; compare {{Galatians 6:2|Galatians 6:2}}). Jesus himself demonstrated perfect humility, gentleness, and patience in his relationships with people.
T

*through the bond of peace:* Paul emphasizes that God accepts both Gentiles and Jews ({{Ephesians 2:11-3:6|2:11–3:6}}). This acceptance should guide behavior. Jews and Gentiles should accept each other in the church (see {{Colossians 3:14-15|Colossians 3:14–15}}).
T

- These three verses might come from an early Christian creed (a formal statement of beliefs). These verses emphasize the unity that all believers share.

- Despite their ethnic differences, Jewish and non-Jewish Christians have one Lord and one faith. Because of this, they should live together in unity. 

- Christ's one body is the church (see {{Ephesians 1:23|1:23}}; {{Ephesians 2:16|2:16}}). 

- *one God and Father of all*: (see {{1 Corinthians 8:6|1 Corinthians 8:6}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:28|15:28}}). 

- *who is over all and through all and in all: *God is especially present in the lives of believers (see {{1 Corinthians 6:19|1 Corinthians 6:19}}; {{2 Corinthians 13:5|2 Corinthians 13:5}}; {{Galatians 2:20|Galatians 2:20}}; {{Colossians 1:27|Colossians 1:27}}; compare {{John 14:16-17|John 14:16–17}}, {{John 14:23|23}}; {{John 15:4-5|15:4–5}}).
T

He has given each of us a gift through his grace to strengthen the community of believers (see {{1 Corinthians 12:7|1 Corinthians 12:7}}; compare {{Romans 12:6|Romans 12:6}}; {{1 Corinthians 12:11|1 Corinthians 12:11}}).
T
Though believers share a common faith, God has given different special abilities to each individual believer for building up the church community.
T

- *"He led captives away"*: This may refer to Christ’s victory over spiritual powers (see {{Ephesians 1:21-22|1:21–22}}; {{Colossians 2:15|Colossians 2:15}}). It may also refer to his capture of disobedient sinners, turning them into believers through the power of the good news. 

- Christ gave gifts to his people (see {{Ephesians 4:11-12|Ephesians 4:11–12}}).
T

*to the lower parts of the earth*: This phrase has been understood in several different ways by Bible scholars. Some people have thought this phrase refers to Jesus' tomb after his crucifixion. Others have suggested it means the world of the dead, the place where spirits go after death (compare {{Matthew 12:40|Matthew 12:40}}; {{1 Peter 3:18-20|1 Peter 3:18–20}}). Still others have connected it to the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost. However, the phrase most likely refers to the incarnation. The incarnation is when Jesus Christ, who is God the Son, descended from heaven and became a human being (see {{John 1:14|John 1:14}}; {{John 3:13|3:13}}; {{Philippians 2:7-8|Philippians 2:7–8}}).
T

- In his letters, Paul provides four different lists of God's gifts (see also {{Romans 12:4-8|Romans 12:4–8}}; {{1 Corinthians 12:8-10|1 Corinthians 12:8–10}}, {{1 Corinthians 12:28|28}}). None of these lists includes all possible gifts. This list focuses on the leadership gifts that help the church grow:

- Apostles are people God sends out as missionary evangelists. They travel around sharing the good news about Jesus.

- Prophets are people who speak messages from God to his people. 

- Evangelists tell others the good news about Jesus. 

- Pastors (which means *shepherds*) are people who take care of God's people (see {{1 Timothy 3:1-7|1 Timothy 3:1–7}}). 

- Teachers are people who explain Scripture and God's truths to the church. 

- The terms *pastors and teachers* might refer to two separate roles, or they might describe two parts of the same role.
T

- God gives gifts to believers to help them strengthen the church (see {{1 Corinthians 12:7|1 Corinthians 12:7}}; compare {{1 Peter 2:5|1 Peter 2:5}}). 

- *to equip the saints for works of ministry*: All believers are called to active Christian service.
T

The goal of ministry is to help all Christians understand and experience their faith more deeply and know God's Son better. When this happens, believers become mature in the Lord (see {{1 Corinthians 2:6|1 Corinthians 2:6}}; {{1 Corinthians 14:20|14:20}}; {{Philippians 3:15|Philippians 3:15}}; {{Colossians 1:28|Colossians 1:28}}; {{Colossians 4:12|4:12}}; compare {{Hebrews 5:14|Hebrews 5:14}}; {{James 1:4|James 1:4}}; {{James 3:2|3:2}}). Christ himself is the standard of maturity. The Holy Spirit's work is to transform people to become fully like Christ ({{Romans 8:29|Romans 8:29}}).
T

*carried around by every wind of teaching*: Mature Christians, with a strong understanding of the good news and of Christ, can identify and resist false teachings (see {{Galatians 1:6-7|Galatians 1:6–7}}; {{Galatians 3:1|3:1}}; {{Colossians 2:8-23|Colossians 2:8–23}}; {{1 Timothy 1:3-7|1 Timothy 1:3–7}}; {{1 Timothy 4:1-3|4:1–3}}; {{1 Timothy 6:3-5|6:3–5}}, {{1 Timothy 6:20|20}}; {{2 Timothy 4:3-4|2 Timothy 4:3–4}}; {{Titus 1:11|Titus 1:11}}).
T

- Each part of the body of Christ has an important role and helps other parts grow. Christ, the head of the body, works through each part. He makes them fit together. He is the ultimate source of growth (see {{Colossians 2:19|Colossians 2:19}}). 

- When all believers serve effectively, the whole body will be healthy, growing, and full of love (compare {{1 Corinthians 8:1|1 Corinthians 8:1}}). Love is the most important factor in Christian growth ({{1 Corinthians 13:1-13|1 Corinthians 13:1–13}}).
T
God's people are called to live in a way that is different from unbelievers in the world.
B

Paul described two ways of living. One was the old way that the believers used to live. It’s the way that people who refuse to trust in God live. This way is marked by sinful desires, actions and words that destroy people.

Sinful desires lead to feelings of anger, hatred and rage. The desires lead to being full of greed and wanting more and more things. Sinful actions include stealing, fighting, committing sexual sins, getting drunk and living wildly. Sinful words include lies and talking about evil and foolish things. Paul described these desires, actions and words as part of a life of darkness.

The other way of living is what Jesus taught. People who live this new life are filled with desires that lead to good things. They are tender and kind to others and forgive them. Their actions do good to others. They work hard and give freely to those in need. Their words also do good. They speak the truth, give thanks to God and build others up. Paul described these desires, actions and words as part of a life of love. They are part of a life of light.

This way of life helps believers stay together as one body. This is part of God’s plan to bring all things together under Jesus’ authority.
T
Paul gives believers specific guidelines for living a new life in Christ.
T

Their minds are full of darkness because their minds are closed and hearts are hard (see {{2 Corinthians 4:4|2 Corinthians 4:4}}). This means they cannot understand spiritual truths clearly. Their minds are "closed," which means they are unwilling or unable to accept God's truth. Their hearts are "hard," which means they have become insensitive to God's guidance.
T

*Having lost all sense of shame*: Unbelievers have hard hearts, meaning they no longer listen to God's guidance. As a result, they lose the ability to know right from wrong. They do not feel guilty about doing sinful things, including sexual immorality (see {{Romans 1:21-31|Romans 1:21–31}}).
T

What you learned about Christ is the truth that comes from him. He gives true understanding (compare {{John 14:6|John 14:6}}). He calls his people to a completely new way of life (compare {{Romans 6:3-14|Romans 6:3–14}}; {{Romans 13:12-14|13:12–14}}; {{Colossians 3:8-10|Colossians 3:8–10}}).
T

*to put on the new self*: God's Spirit shows his life within the believer (see {{Colossians 3:10|Colossians 3:10}}; compare {{Genesis 1:26|Genesis 1:26}}; {{Romans 12:1-2|Romans 12:1–2}}; {{Galatians 5:22-23|Galatians 5:22–23}}). The transforming work of God's Spirit is part of the gift of salvation ({{Ephesians 2:8-10|Ephesians 2:8–10}}).
T

- *speak truthfully to his neighbor: *(compare {{Zechariah 8:16|Zechariah 8:16}}). 

- *we are all members of one another:* (see {{Romans 12:5|Romans 12:5}}; {{1 Corinthians 12:12-13|1 Corinthians 12:12–13}}, {{1 Corinthians 12:27|27}}).
T

- *"Be angry, yet do not sin":* This verse quotes {{Psalm 4:4|Psalm 4:4}}. The literal form of the quotation does not justify anger. Anger gives the devil an way to influence us (see {{James 1:20|James 1:20}}). God's people should be gentle and gracious, not harsh or angry (see {{Ephesians 4:31-32|Ephesians 4:31–32}}). 

- *Do not let the sun set upon your anger*: This means we should resolve our anger quickly. We should not allow our anger continue or grow stronger.
T
Christians should work hard, be honest, and care for others (see {{1 Thessalonians 4:11|1 Thessalonians 4:11}}; {{2 Thessalonians 3:6-12|2 Thessalonians 3:6–12}}).
T
Believers should learn new ways of speaking that encourage others (see also {{Ephesians 5:3-4|5:3–4}}, {{Ephesians 5:12|12}}).
T

- Believers must not offend or push away God’s Holy Spirit, who shows that they belong to God (see {{Mark 3:29|Mark 3:29}}; {{Acts 5:3-5|Acts 5:3–5}}, {{Acts 5:9|9}}; {{1 Thessalonians 4:8|1 Thessalonians 4:8}}; {{Hebrews 6:4-8|Hebrews 6:4–8}}). 

- *in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption*: The Spirit's presence confirms that believers belong to God and guarantees their future salvation (see {{Ephesians 1:13-14|Ephesians 1:13–14}}; {{Romans 8:16-17|Romans 8:16–17}}; {{2 Corinthians 1:22|2 Corinthians 1:22}}; {{1 John 4:13|1 John 4:13}}).
T

Forgiving others who share your faith is a natural and positive response to experiencing God's forgiving grace through Christ (compare {{Colossians 3:12-13|Colossians 3:12–13}}; {{1 John 4:19|1 John 4:19}}).
T

- *Be imitators of God*: We imitate God mainly by showing love ({{Ephesians 5:2|5:2}}; see {{Matthew 5:44-45|Matthew 5:44–45}}, {{Matthew 5:48|48}}). 

- *as beloved children*: Just as children follow their parents' example, believers should follow God's example ({{1 Corinthians 4:14-17|1 Corinthians 4:14–17}}).
T

- Christ's love is shown especially in his sacrifice for us (compare {{Ephesians 5:25|5:25}}; {{John 15:13|John 15:13}}; {{Romans 5:8|Romans 5:8}}). Christian love follows Christ's example of sacrificial love (see {{Philippians 2:5-8|Philippians 2:5–8}}). 

- Paul uses Old Testament imagery, where the smell of a burning *fragrant sacrificial offering* was pleasing to God (see {{Leviticus 1:9|Leviticus 1:9}}; {{Leviticus 2:2|2:2}}; compare {{Romans 12:1|Romans 12:1}}).
T

God's people, also called *the saints* or *holy ones*, should live a holy life. They must avoid the immoral behavior common among unbelievers (compare {{Ephesians 4:19|4:19}}; {{Colossians 3:5|Colossians 3:5}}).
T
God’s people should speak in ways that show they are thankful to God (see {{Ephesians 4:29|4:29}}; {{Ephesians 5:3|5:3}}, {{Ephesians 5:12|12}}).
T

- Many similar statements describe the type of person who will not inherit *the kingdom of Christ and of God:* See {{1 Corinthians 6:9-10|1 Corinthians 6:9–10}}; {{Galatians 5:19-21|Galatians 5:19–21}}; {{Revelation 22:15|Revelation 22:15}}; compare {{Colossians 3:5-6|Colossians 3:5–6}}. 

- a *greedy person (that is, an idolater):* The things greedy people desire become their gods (see {{Matthew 6:24|Matthew 6:24}}).
T
God's anger will come during his final judgment (see {{Romans 1:18|Romans 1:18}}; {{Colossians 3:5-6|Colossians 3:5–6}}; compare {{John 3:36|John 3:36}}).
T
*do not be partakers*: Compare {{2 Corinthians 6:14-7:1|2 Corinthians 6:14–7:1}}.
T

- *Darkness* means not knowing God and being controlled by sin (see {{Ephesians 4:18|4:18}}). 

- *Light in the Lord* is the good news of Christ (see {{John 8:12|John 8:12}}). As people of light, believers live in fellowship with God, who has no darkness (see {{1 John 1:5-7|1 John 1:5–7}}; {{1 John 5:9|5:9}}; compare {{Matthew 5:14-16|Matthew 5:14–16}}; {{John 8:12|John 8:12}}; {{John 12:35-36|12:35–36}}, {{John 12:46|46}}; {{Romans 13:12|Romans 13:12}}; {{2 Corinthians 6:14|2 Corinthians 6:14}}; {{1 Thessalonians 5:4-8|1 Thessalonians 5:4–8}}; {{1 Peter 2:9|1 Peter 2:9}}).
T

God's people should do what is good, right, and true. This is in agreement with God's light (compare {{Romans 12:2|Romans 12:2}}; some early manuscripts use *Spirit* instead of *light*; compare {{Ephesians 4:22-24|Ephesians 4:22–24}}; {{Matthew 7:16-20|Matthew 7:16–20}}; {{Galatians 5:22-23|Galatians 5:22–23}}).
T
*Test and prove what pleases the Lord*: The goal is to obey God's will, not simply to understand it (see {{Romans 12:2|Romans 12:2}}; {{Philippians 1:10|Philippians 1:10}}).
T

*but rather expose them*: This does not mean to accuse or condemn people with words (see {{1 Corinthians 5:9-13|1 Corinthians 5:9–13}}). Instead, it means to show what is wrong by living in a way that reflects God’s light (see {{John 3:20-21|John 3:20–21}}; {{Romans 13:12|Romans 13:12}}; {{1 Peter 2:9|1 Peter 2:9}}),
T

*"Wake up, O sleeper"*: This could be words from an unknown Christian song. It might be inspired by texts in Isaiah (compare {{Isaiah 26:19|Isaiah 26:19}}; {{Isaiah 52:1|52:1}}; {{Isaiah 60:1|60:1}}). It urges God's people to leave their sinful ways and live in the full light of Christ.
T
Foolish people do not understand God and his ways. Wise people know God and understand his ways (see {{Job 28:28|Job 28:28}}; {{Proverbs 1:7|Proverbs 1:7}}; {{Proverbs 2:1-22|2:1–22}}).
T

- *redeeming the time*: See also {{Colossians 4:5|Colossians 4:5}}. 

- *the days are evi*l: see {{Matthew 24:6-12|Matthew 24:6–12}}, {{Matthew 24:15-22|15–22}}; {{2 Thessalonians 2:3-10|2 Thessalonians 2:3–10}}.
T

- The Holy Spirit, not wine, should have the most influence in the lives of believers (see {{Proverbs 23:29-35|Proverbs 23:29–35}}; compare {{Acts 2:15-18|Acts 2:15–18}}). 

- *be filled*: The grammar here suggests a repeated, ongoing process of letting the Holy Spirit guide and influence the lives of believers, not a single event.
T

- *with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs*: Lives filled with the Holy Spirit will show themselves through singing and making music ({{Colossians 3:16-17|Colossians 3:16–17}}). Joyful praise, worship, and giving thanks are good responses to God's saving grace. 

- *Speak to one another*: Singing together strengthens the body of Christ. 

- The Lord hears the music in our hearts. The Lord knows and values our sincere worship, even when it is not expressed out loud but comes from deep inside us.

- *In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ*: Jesus Christ is our mediator and representative as we approach God (compare {{John 14:13-14|John 14:13–14}}; {{John 16:23-27|16:23–27}}; {{Revelation 22:4|Revelation 22:4}}).
T

- *Submit to one another*: The verb form connects it with the command to *be filled* ({{Ephesians 5:18|5:18}}). This general instruction (compare {{Philippians 2:3|Philippians 2:3}}) applies to all three relationships Paul discusses: 

- wives and husbands ({{Ephesians 5:22-33|Ephesians 5:22–33}}), 

- children and parents ({{Ephesians 6:1-4|6:1–4}}), and 

- slaves and masters ({{Ephesians 6:5-9|6:5–9}}). 

Believers express submission not out of fear or personal gain, but out of respect for Christ.
B

Paul taught how people in God’s family must treat their human family. In Paul’s time, families usually included a husband, a wife, children and slaves. Men had the most authority in the family. Women, children and slaves had to obey them.

Yet serving Jesus as Lord changed the way people acted in their families. They had to follow Jesus’ example. Jesus is a leader who serves and he sacrificed himself for the good of others. Every member of the family was to treat one another with love and respect. The one who had the most authority in the family was Jesus.

Paul called God the Master of all believers. He reminded them that God didn’t treat any one believer as more important than another. Men, women, children and slaves were all part of the church. The church is so important to Jesus that Paul described the relationship like a marriage. The church being joined closely to Jesus is part of God’s plan. It shows God’s desire to save the whole world.
T

Paul provides clear guidance on how believers should interact in a Christian home (see also {{Colossians 3:18-4:1|Colossians 3:18–4:1}}; {{1 Peter 2:18-3:7|1 Peter 2:18–3:7}}). Love and respect should define all relationships among believers as a way to show their commitment to the Lord.
T

A wife’s Christian commitment includes choosing to submit to her husband as part of living out her faith (see {{1 Corinthians 11:3-10|1 Corinthians 11:3–10}}; {{1 Corinthians 14:34-35|14:34–35}}; {{Colossians 3:18|Colossians 3:18}}; {{1 Timothy 2:11-12|1 Timothy 2:11–12}}; {{Titus 2:5|Titus 2:5}}; {{1 Peter 3:1-6|1 Peter 3:1–6}}). At the same time, all Christians (including husbands and wives) are called to submit to one another out of respect for Christ ({{Ephesians 5:21|Ephesians 5:21}}). At the same time, husbands are called to love their wives and care for them sacrificially, following the example of Christ (see {{Ephesians 5:21-23|Ephesians 5:21–23}}). This mutual submission, respect, and love build a healthy, God-honoring marriage.
T

Christian wives should respect and submit to their husbands. Equally important, Christian husbands should love their wives (see {{Colossians 3:18-19|Colossians 3:18–19}}). Christian marriages reflect the union and relationship between the Lord and the church.
T

- *For the husband is the head of the wife*: To be the head is to have authority (see {{1 Corinthians 11:3|1 Corinthians 11:3}}). 

- *as Christ is the head of the church*: See {{Ephesians 1:22|Ephesians 1:22}}; {{Ephesians 4:15|4:15}}; {{Colossians 1:18|Colossians 1:18}}; {{Colossians 2:10|2:10}}, {{Colossians 2:19|19}}.
T

Christian husbands should love their wives just as Christ loved the church. This means loving sacrificially, for Christ gave up his life for the church ({{Ephesians 5:2|5:2}}; compare {{Colossians 3:19|Colossians 3:19}}; {{1 Peter 3:7|1 Peter 3:7}}).
T

*by the washing with water through the word*: The church has been purified by the message of good news. God has forgiven the sins of his people through Christ's sacrificial death ({{John 15:3|John 15:3}}; compare {{Titus 3:5|Titus 3:5}}; {{1 Peter 3:21|1 Peter 3:21}}).
T

*a glorious church, without stain or wrinkle or any such blemish*: The church's sins are forgiven through Christ's sacrifice, and the Holy Spirit purifies her life. As a result, the church stands holy and without fault before God. Compare {{Ephesians 1:4|1:4}}; {{2 Corinthians 11:2|2 Corinthians 11:2}}; {{Colossians 1:22|Colossians 1:22}}; {{Revelation 19:7-8|Revelation 19:7–8}}; {{Revelation 21:2|21:2}}.
T

Husbands should value and care for their wives as they do themselves. In marriage, the two become one (see {{Ephesians 5:31|5:31}}). This means that caring for one’s wife is like caring for one’s own body.
T
The unity of husband and wife should motivate the husband to care for his wife.
T
*This mystery is profound*: Both the unity of husband and wife and the unity of Christ and the church are a great mystery(see study note on 1:8–10).
T
Paul summarizes his teaching on the relationship between husbands and wives ({{Ephesians 5:22-33|5:22–33}}). Christian marriages should be marked by love and respect.
T

The relationship between parents and children should reflect their devotion to the Lord. Christian children should obey their parents, and Christian parents should discipline their children gently (see {{Colossians 3:20-21|Colossians 3:20–21}}).
T
Children who honor and respect their parents also honor and respect God. This leads to blessings.
T

- *Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath*: Fathers can make their children angry by being harsh or unfair (see {{Colossians 3:21|Colossians 3:21}}). 

- *bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord*: Parents should teach their children discipline and lessons from the Lord so they learn a good way of living that pleases God. This discipline should be loving and gentle. It should not be excessive, so that children are not turned away from the Lord but are drawn to him (compare {{Hebrews 12:5-11|Hebrews 12:5–11}}).
T

Obeying human masters shows a Christian slave's service to Christ (see {{Colossians 3:22-23|Colossians 3:22–23}}; {{1 Timothy 6:1-2|1 Timothy 6:1–2}}; {{Titus 2:9-10|Titus 2:9–10}}; {{1 Peter 2:18-23|1 Peter 2:18–23}}).
T

- The relationship between slaves and masters (and similarly, between employees and employers) should be guided by their commitment to the Lord and their desire to support each other in Christ. Christian slaves should obey their masters, and Christian masters should treat their slaves kindly (see {{Colossians 3:22-4:1|Colossians 3:22–4:1}}). 

- Paul was not promoting slavery. Paul was teaching Christians how to live with it as a reality in that culture (for Paul’s views on slavery, see Philemon Book Introduction, "Meaning and Message").
T

*as servants of Christ*: Believers have been bought by Christ's sacrifice. Because of this, believers do not belong to themselves anymore (see {{1 Corinthians 6:19-20|1 Corinthians 6:19–20}}; {{1 Corinthians 7:22|7:22}}; compare {{Romans 1:1|Romans 1:1}}; {{Galatians 1:10|Galatians 1:10}}; {{Philippians 1:1|Philippians 1:1}}). For Christian slaves, God's will is for them to honor him by serving their human masters faithfully and with entusiasm.
T
The Bible uses the image of a master to describe the Lord’s authority over believers. He will reward those who are faithful (see {{1 Corinthians 3:12-15|1 Corinthians 3:12–15}}).
T

- *do the same*: Act with integrity and care for the well-being of others (see {{Colossians 4:1|Colossians 4:1}}). 

- *Give up your use of threats*: Christian masters will also answer to the same Master in heaven for their actions on earth. Pleasing God means treating their slaves humanely and kindly.

- *there is no favoritism with Him*: God judges everyone by the same standard (see {{Deuteronomy 10:17|Deuteronomy 10:17}}; {{Acts 10:34|Acts 10:34}}; {{Romans 2:11|Romans 2:11}}; {{Colossians 3:25|Colossians 3:25}}). God’s justice affirms the dignity of all people and calls for their freedom.
T
Paul's final message reminds believers about the devil's opposition. Paul urges believers to protect themselves with all of God's armor.
B

The devil’s plan for the world is evil. It’s the opposite of God’s plan to bring heaven and earth together under Jesus.

On the cross, Jesus won the victory over the powers of evil, sin and death. That is the good news of peace that Paul talked about. Jesus doesn’t yet rule completely over all the earth. Until he does, the devil continues trying to stop God’s plan.

Paul described this like a spiritual fight between the spiritual forces of evil and God. God’s people are part of this battle. God gives them spiritual armour and weapons to help them. Believers can trust in God’s power to save them from evil. God’s power also makes them able to pray.

The believers’ prayers helped Paul to share the good news about Jesus boldly. Paul ended his letter with a blessing for the believers he was writing to. The blessing reminded them of how to be part of God’s plan for the world. They received peace, love and faith from God. This allowed them to live together as a family that loves and serves Jesus.
T

*Put on the full armor of God*: See {{Romans 13:12|Romans 13:12}}; {{2 Corinthians 10:4-5|2 Corinthians 10:4–5}}. Only with the Lord's protection can a believer resist all of the devil's plans (compare {{1 Peter 5:8-9|1 Peter 5:8–9}}).
T

Believers should not see other people as their enemies. Instead, their opposition comes from spiritual evil in the unseen world. Christ has authority over that realm (see {{Ephesians 1:21-22|1:21–22}}).
T
God's armor helps believers resist the devil's attacks during times when evil seems strong, allowing them to stand firm.
T

*the breastplate of righteousness*: A breastplate is a piece of armor that covers the chest to protect the heart and other vital organs during battle. In the Bible, Paul uses this image to show how righteousness—being right with God and living in a right way—protects a believer’s heart and life from the attacks of the devil. This righteousness is either:

- the righteousness God gives to those who believe in Christ, or

- the righteous way of life that the Spirit of God creates in believers. 

Each one suggests the presence of the other.
T

Paul uses the armor worn by Roman soldiers as a metaphor for the spiritual armor of believers. Most of this armor is for defense, not attack. Paul is not mainly focused on the exact use of each piece, but on the gifts God gives to protect his people. Trusting in Christ and knowing the Scriptures help believers stand firm against the devil’s attacks (compare {{James 4:7|James 4:7}}; {{1 Peter 5:8-9|1 Peter 5:8–9}}).
T
*your feet fitted with the readiness of the gospel of peace*: This means letting peace from the good news (the gospel) guide your life (see {{Romans 5:1|Romans 5:1}}).
T

- *the shield of faith*: Faith means trusting Christ as Savior or trusting God to meet needs during difficult times. Like a shield that protects a soldier from arrows, faith protects believers from fear, doubt, and the lies of the devil.

- *all the flaming arrows*: Paul uses a strong picture to describe how temptation to sin can come suddenly and powerfully (compare {{Matthew 6:13|Matthew 6:13}}; {{Matthew 26:41|26:41}}; {{1 Corinthians 10:13|1 Corinthians 10:13}}; {{James 1:12-15|James 1:12–15}}). In battle, arrows were sometimes dipped in pitch and set on fire before being shot. In the same way, the devil sends dangerous temptations, but faith in God can stop them.
T

- *take the helmet of salvation*: Just like a helmet protects a soldier’s head, the assurance of salvation protects a believer’s mind. It reminds believers that God has saved them and given them eternal life through faith in Christ.

- *the sword of the Spirit*: This is the word of God. It is like a weapon believers use to answer attacks, either by sharing the good news about Jesus, or by speaking or remembering what God has said in Scripture (compare {{Jeremiah 23:29|Jeremiah 23:29}}; {{Hebrews 4:12|Hebrews 4:12}}). A sword is a weapon with a long, sharp blade used in battle.
T

- Paul shows the difference between mental prayer and prayer in the Spirit. Prayer in the Spirit is prayer that is led by the Spirit of God living within believers. (see {{1 Corinthians 14:15|1 Corinthians 14:15}}; {{Jude 20|Jude 1:20}}; compare {{Romans 8:26-27|Romans 8:26–27}}). 

- *every kind of prayer and petition*: Believers should make prayer a part of daily life, turning all of life into prayer (see {{Philippians 4:6-7|Philippians 4:6–7}}; {{1 Thessalonians 5:17|1 Thessalonians 5:17}}). This is not just for themselves, but for all believers everywhere. 

- *stay alert with all perseverance*: The danger of the devil is constant.
T

- Paul's mission was to help non-Jews (Gentiles) understand they are now accepted by God and welcomed into God's church. 

- *the mystery of the gospel*: See study notes on 1:8–10; 3:3. 

- *I am an ambassador in chain*s: Although writing as a prisoner (see {{Ephesians 3:1|3:1}}; {{Ephesians 4:1|4:1}}), Paul knew his role as God's ambassador was to continue speaking boldly for God (compare {{2 Corinthians 5:20|2 Corinthians 5:20}}) .
T
Paul ends this letter with personal words and a blessing that repeats the desires expressed at the beginning of the letter.
T

- *Peace … love … faith … grace*: These qualities are mentioned at the start of the letter ({{Ephesians 1:2|1:2}}, {{Ephesians 1:15|15}}). Peace, love, faith, and grace are what Paul most desired for believers.

- *to the brothers:* Paul uses this term to refer to all members of the same family, both male and female. 

- *to all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with an undying love: *Another way of translating this is "be eternally upon all who love our Lord Jesus Christ."
